The essential con of economics is instilling the cultural belief that it is a natural system based in immutable, scientific, laws and not something that simply came out of people's heads ad hoc. This is why economists love to appropriate the language of hard science--particularly evolutionary biology--to lend their notions credibility. Because if we accept that economics is a social construct--an economism--we must, as participants in it, accept some responsibility for those the system fails or exploits. Do you not believe in economic laws, such as the law of demand or the law of supply, then?

Economics is indeed not a natural science; but it's a social science. It observes human society and makes predictions about the general trends which are generally correct. For instance, it's generally correct that, if I as a seller raise the price of a good, there are going to be less people who will buy it from me. There are exceptions - such as with irrational cases such as charity - but the general trend holds true.

As for economics being a social construct, I'm not so sure. I think what you're trying to say is that a free market is a social construct, which is correct as far as I know. The failure of the free market, however, is not the failure of economics. Many economists starting from the age of Keynes and harking up to the modern world have proposed how the free market cannot be used extensively to solve every single problem - market failure is well documented and understood as a fact within the study of economics. What free market economists disagree on with anti-free market ideologists, is the extent to which market failure is an issue compared to other forms of allocations of goods. Free market economists may think that government allocation of resources is even more problematic than the allocation as given by the free market, but that doesn't mean that the free market economist blindly believes in the good of the free market or that the free market can do no wrong.

As for the final question of whether economics should be above ethics, nobody ever said it should be - it's simply not related to ethics. Economics is a study of how we can use human self-interest to create a better world, and how self-interest and greed makes the world go round. There's nothing in economics to suggest that its laws are above ethics - because simply put, financial transactions do not carry a moral quality. If you buy a loaf of bread from a baker's, it's not a moral decision but an economic one. Hence, economics is generally not related to morality, which is why some economists do not think that the study of morality has to be linked to economics. Recently however, as high-profile philosopher Michael Sandel has argued, our world has began to move from a free market economy to a market society, and there is indeed a possible future in which economists will have to grapple with more complex moral question alongside fundamental economic questions - if that is your worry, then I'd suggest that you read one of his books "What Money Can't Buy, the moral limits of markets", which argues for a lot of the things you argue for. His lectures and speeches on the subject are also brilliant and I would recommend them to you if you ever want to see more about ethics in economics.

Economics is a study of how we can use human self-interest to create a better world, and how self-interest and greed makes the world go round. [...] if you buy a loaf of bread from a baker's, it's not a moral decision but an economic one. Hence, economics is generally not related to morality

I think you are somewhat misunderstanding (or at least mis-stating) the case here. Human actions and decisions are not split between the economic and the moral. All actions can legitimately be considered from an ethical point of view. If the baker chooses to sell the loaf to you, for the highest price he can get, rather than (say) giving it to the starving, homeless orphan in the street outside, that is a moral decision as well as an economic one (and by bringing in the starving orphan I am merely trying to emphasize the point; it was always a moral decision as well as an economic one, even before he came into the picture). If someone chooses between two job offers:- one designing medical devices, and one designing torture devices - that is a moral choice as well as an economic one.

The proper distinction then, is that economic science, as such, is purely descriptive, not prescriptive. The economist, when speaking strictly as a scientist, does not impose his value judgments on the facts of reality. He is concerned with what people really do, or with what they could do, but never with what they ought to do.

This does not mean, of course, that an economist cannot express an opinion, informed by his economic understanding, about what someone ought to do. But in doing so he goes beyond the scope of strict, value-free economics, since he must rely on ethical premises in addition to economic ones.

Do you accept that an objective reality exists? Do you accept that there are knowable, objective physical laws?

If so, do you further accept that human beings and their actions are part of the physical universe and hence subject to the objective laws of physical reality?

Economic science, "may be defined [...] as the study of the material world and of the activities and mutual relations of men so far as all these are the objective conditions to the gratification and to the welfare of men." (Frank A. Fetter, Economic Principles)

The objective conditions to human welfare are not a "social construct." A particular economic theory may be wrong, but this can only be decided by evidence and reason, not by emotional rejection.
